doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Making written music sound improvised
summary: Hyman thinks all piano music, from Joplin to Mozart, should sound as if improvised in the moment.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I believe one of your most recent recordings was a Gershwin collection? I’m curious as to, from a technical standpoint, what have you found was one of your most challenging prospects? Because when you record Scott Joplin, this is music that’s pretty much written out, yet it has to be played like it doesn’t sound like it’s written.

I think that all piano music, not just jazz, not just Scott Joplin, but classical music in general, it should sound as though the performer is improvising it. That’s what I think. And at its best, in my judgment, I can convince myself in an irrational way, that that is happening. And if you hear Mozart played that way, it sounds like the performer might be improvising it. We know they’re not. But there are aspects of performance that even people who are playing note for note understand. And it has to sound as though it’s happening at that moment.
